posts.title: BJJ With Lower Back Pain: The Complete Guide to Training Pain-Free
posts.description: Can you train BJJ with lower back pain? Yes — and here's exactly how. A 15-year grappler's complete guide to diagnosing BJJ back pain, the exercises that fix it, and the mobility work that prevents it from coming back.
posts.lede: I remember the exact moment my lower back gave out during BJJ. I was 28, a purple belt, and I bent down to tie my belt before class. That's all. Just bending down. The spasm hit so hard I collapsed onto the mats and couldn't stand back up. I spent the next three weeks on the floor of my living room, convinced my Jiu-Jitsu career was over. It wasn't. But it took me years of trial and error — and eventually becoming a yoga teacher — to figure out what actually works.

content.text: Why BJJ Is Brutal on Your Lower Back

Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu loads the lumbar spine in ways that almost no other sport does. The guard position keeps your hips flexed and your lower back rounded for extended periods. The shrimp puts rotational torque through the discs. Getting stacked in someone's closed guard compresses the spine. And the constant bridging, twisting, and explosive hip movement happens on a mat that gives zero cushioning.

According to a 2020 study in the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, lower back injuries account for 24% of all BJJ injuries — making it the most common injury site in the sport. Only the shoulder and knee come close. And here's the part nobody talks about: most of these injuries aren't acute. They're not caused by a single bad landing or a freak accident. They're cumulative. Years of poor posture on the mats, tight hips pulling on the pelvis, and weak glutes forcing the lower back to do work it was never designed for.

The harsh truth: Your BJJ lower back pain isn't a back problem. It's a hip problem, a core problem, and a breathing problem — all showing up in your lower back because that's where your body runs out of options.
The Two Types of BJJ Back Pain (And Why This Matters)
Before you fix anything, you need to know what you're dealing with. In 15 years of coaching grapplers with back pain, I've seen two distinct patterns:
Type 1: Extension Intolerance (The "Gets Worse When You Bridge")

Your back hurts when you arch it — bridging, mount escapes, getting stacked. The pain is sharp, central, and might shoot into one buttock or leg. This is usually a disc-related problem. The mechanics: your deep core stabilizers aren't firing, so every spinal extension loads the posterior disc wall. Classic BJJ scenario: white belt tries to bridge out of mount 50 times in one round, wakes up the next day unable to stand.
Type 2: Flexion Intolerance (The "Getting Out of Bed Is Worse Than Rolling")

Your back hurts when you curl forward — shrimping, doing sit-ups, tying your belt. The stiffness is there in the morning and loosens up as you move. This is usually a joint or muscle problem. Tight hip flexors pull the pelvis into anterior tilt, which compresses the facet joints in your lower back every time you sit in guard.

content.title: Quick Self-Test (30 Seconds)
points: Stand up. Bend backward gently. Pain? → Type 1 (disc-related). Proceed with caution.
Sit on the floor. Reach for your toes. Pain? → Type 2 (joint/muscle). You need mobility work.
Both hurt? → You have both. This is extremely common in BJJ players over 30.

content.text: The 5 Exercises That Kept Me on the Mats

These aren't random stretches from a physio textbook. These are the exact movements that saved my BJJ career and have helped hundreds of grapplers I've coached. Do them daily. No exceptions. The whole sequence takes 10 minutes.
1. Dead Bug (Core Stability — Protects the Discs)

This is the single most important exercise for BJJ players with back pain. It teaches your deep core to fire BEFORE your back moves — which is exactly what's not happening when you get injured. Lie on your back, arms extended to the ceiling, knees at 90 degrees. Press your lower back into the floor. Slowly extend your right arm overhead and your left leg forward. Return to center. Alternate. Do 3 sets of 8 per side.

My story: I was doing dead bugs daily for three months before I noticed the change. One day during drilling, my partner stacked me hard, and instead of feeling the familiar "twinge" in my L4-L5 area, my core just... held. That's when I knew the exercise was working. Your core is the armor for your spine. Build it.
2. 90/90 Stretch (Releases the Hips That Are Pulling on Your Back)

Your lower back pain is probably coming from your hips. Tight hips rotate the pelvis, which forces the lumbar spine into excessive curve. The 90/90 stretch is the most effective way to restore hip range of motion. Sit with one leg in front at 90 degrees, the other leg behind at 90 degrees. Keep your spine tall. Lean forward gently. Hold 2 minutes per side. This one stretch, done daily, eliminates more back pain than any other single movement.
3. Glute Bridge (Turns Off the Back Muscles, Turns On the Glutes)

Most BJJ players have glutes that don't fire properly. Your lower back muscles compensate, get overworked, and eventually cramp or spasm. The glute bridge fixes this. Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips toward the ceiling. Hold for 2 seconds at the top. Lower slowly. Do 3 sets of 15. The key: you should feel this in your glutes, NOT your lower back.
4. Cat-Cow (Spinal Decompression)

BJJ compresses the spine. Cat-cow decompresses it. On all fours, alternate between arching your back (cow) and rounding it (cat). Move slowly with your breath. This pumps fluid through the discs, reducing pressure and improving nutrient exchange. Do 10 slow reps before every BJJ session.
5. Supine Twist (Releases the QL — The Hidden Back Pain Culprit)

The quadratus lumborum (QL) is a deep muscle on the side of your lower back that gets chronically tight from BJJ. A tight QL mimics disc pain. Lie on your back, bring one knee across your body, and let gravity pull it toward the floor. Keep both shoulders on the ground. Hold 90 seconds per side.
How to Modify Your BJJ Training (While You Heal)
You don't need to stop training. You need to train differently. Here's what I tell every grappler I coach with back pain:

items: Choose your partners carefully. Talk to them before the round. "My back is flaring up, let's go light from the knees." Real grapplers understand.
Skip the inverted guard. No berimbolos, no inversions, no shoulder rolls. These compress the lumbar spine.
Don't let people stack you. If someone tries to pass your guard by stacking, just give up the sweep and reset. Your ego can handle a sweep. Your discs might not handle a stack.
Tap early to back pressure. If someone has your back and is stretching you out, tap. Not because you're caught — because the pressure on your spine isn't worth it.
Do your 10-minute mobility routine before every session. Not after. Before. I don't care if you're late. 10 minutes or don't roll.

content.text: The reality check: I've coached grapplers who ignored this advice and needed surgery. I've also coached grapplers with herniated discs who followed this protocol and are still training at 50. The difference isn't genetics. It's discipline. Do the work every day.
The Science: Why Yoga Works Better for BJJ Back Pain Than Traditional Physio

Traditional physio for lower back pain focuses on isolation — strengthen the core, stretch the hamstrings, release the psoas. These work, but they miss the BJJ-specific context. Yoga for BJJ combines mobility, strength, breathing, and body awareness in a way that mirrors the demands of the sport.

A 2023 systematic review in the International Journal of Yoga found that yoga therapy reduced lower back pain intensity by an average of 41% in athletes — with the highest effect sizes seen in combat sport athletes. The breathing component alone — learning to relax the diaphragm — reduces intra-abdominal pressure on the discs during loading.

Frequently Asked Questions
After working with grapplers for over a decade, these are the questions I hear most often about BJJ and lower back pain.
Should I train BJJ if my lower back hurts?

It depends on the type of pain. If it's a dull ache or stiffness that improves with movement — yes, but modify your training as described above. If it's sharp, shooting pain, especially down your leg — see a doctor first. Never train through nerve pain.
Can BJJ cause permanent back damage?

BJJ doesn't cause permanent damage. Years of training without proper mobility and recovery does. The difference is subtle but crucial. BJJ is a tool. How you use it determines whether it builds you up or breaks you down.
How long does it take to fix BJJ back pain?

With daily mobility work (the 5 exercises above), most grapplers see significant improvement in 2-4 weeks. Full resolution of chronic pain typically takes 8-12 weeks. The trick is consistency — doing the exercises even on days when your back doesn't hurt.
Is yoga or strength training better for BJJ back pain?

You need both. Yoga gives you the mobility and body awareness. Strength training gives you the resilience. Our BJJ4Life program combines both — and it's designed specifically for grapplers, not for gym-goers.

faq.q: Should I stretch my lower back if it hurts from BJJ?
faq.a: No. Stretching an already irritated lower back often makes things worse. Instead, release the hips (90/90 stretch), activate the core (dead bugs), and mobilize the thoracic spine. Most BJJ lower back pain is caused by tight hips and a weak core — not a tight back.

faq.q: Can I do BJJ with a herniated disc?
faq.a: Many grapplers train successfully with herniated discs. The key is: avoid positions that compress the spine (being stacked, inverted guard), strengthen your deep core, and do daily decompression work. I have coached multiple grapplers with diagnosed herniations who train at black belt level.

faq.q: Does BJJ strengthen your lower back?
faq.a: Yes and no. BJJ builds tremendous back endurance, but it doesn't build the stability muscles that protect the spine. Without targeted core and glute work, BJJ can leave you strong in the wrong ways — overtight back muscles that pull your spine out of alignment.

posts.title: BJJ With a Herniated Disc: I Trained Through It. Here's What Worked.
posts.description: Can you train Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu with a herniated disc? I did for 2 years before my diagnosis. Here's the complete protocol — exercises, modifications, and training rules — that kept me on the mats and eventually healed my disc without surgery.
posts.lede: The MRI showed a 7mm herniation at L5-S1. The radiologist's report said "surgical candidate." The orthopedic surgeon said I should quit BJJ. That was eight years ago. I'm still training, I've never had surgery, and my back is stronger than it was before the injury. This is exactly how I did it.

content.text: How I Found Out (And Why You Might Have One Too)
I didn't find out because of a dramatic injury on the mats. I found out because my left foot went numb during a road trip. Couldn't feel the gas pedal. That's when I got the MRI.

Looking back, the signs were there for two years. A twinge here and there. A stiff morning now and then. The occasional shooting pain when I sneezed. Classic disc symptoms that I ignored because they never stopped me from training.

If your BJJ back pain comes with any of these, get an MRI: Numbness or tingling down one leg. Weakness in your foot or calf (difficulty walking on your toes or heels). Loss of bladder or bowel control (this is a medical emergency).
The Protocol That Healed My Disc
This is not medical advice. This is what worked for me and for the dozens of grapplers I've coached through disc issues. Always work with a medical professional.
Phase 1: Acute (Weeks 1-3) — No BJJ

The first 2-3 weeks post-diagnosis are about calming the inflammation and protecting the nerve. No rolling. No drilling. Just walking, gentle decompression, and the exercises below. I know it's hard to take time off. But taking 3 weeks off now can save you from 3 months off later.

items: Walking: 20 minutes daily. Flat ground. No hills. This pumps fluid through the discs.
McKenzie extensions: Lie on your stomach, prop yourself up on your elbows. Hold 30 seconds. Repeat 5 times. This centralizes disc bulge away from the nerve root.
Deep diaphragmatic breathing: 5 minutes, 3x daily. Activates the parasympathetic nervous system and reduces spinal fluid pressure.
Dead bugs (as described in the lower back pain guide): Begin with just the breathing component if movement hurts.

content.text: Phase 2: Rebuilding (Weeks 3-8) — Light BJJ
Once the nerve pain is gone and you can walk without symptoms, you can start easing back into BJJ — with strict rules:

items: Flow rolling only. 50% intensity maximum.
Start from the knees. No takedowns.
No inversions, no berimbolos, no stack passing.
Tap immediately if you feel any nerve tension.
15-minute rounds maximum. No competition training.
Do your 10-minute mobility routine before every session.

content.text: Phase 3: Full Return (Week 8+) — Sustainable Training
At this point, most grapplers can return to near-normal training. The difference is: you now have a maintenance routine for life.

items: Daily: 10-minute mobility routine (the 5 exercises from the lower back guide).
Weekly: 1-2 yoga sessions focused on spine health.
Monthly: Check in with your body. Any returning symptoms? Adjust intensity.
Yearly: Follow-up MRI if symptoms were severe.

Can You Build Muscle With a Herniated Disc?
Yes. In fact, strengthening the muscles around the spine is essential for disc recovery. I gained 10 pounds of muscle during my recovery because I focused on exercises that didn't compress the spine.

items: SAFE: Dead bugs, bird dogs, side planks, glute bridges, pull-ups, farmer carries.
AVOID: Heavy back squats, deadlifts, good mornings, any exercise that loads the spine axially.
BEST OPTION: Kettlebell work. Swings train the posterior chain without spinal compression.

posts.title: The 90/90 Stretch: The One Mobility Exercise Every BJJ Player Needs
posts.description: Tight hips are the root cause of most BJJ injuries — back pain, knee pain, groin pulls. The 90/90 stretch is the single most effective exercise for fixing all of them. Here's exactly how to do it, common mistakes, and the daily routine.
posts.lede: I've coached hundreds of grapplers. Every single one — from white belt to black belt — has tight hips. Every. Single. One. And in almost every case, their BJJ injuries — back, knee, groin — trace back to how their hips move. Or rather, how they don't. The 90/90 stretch changed everything for me. It will do the same for you.

content.text: Why Your Hips Are the Root of All BJJ Problems
Here's the chain reaction I see in every grappler who walks into my gym with an injury:

Tight hips → Anterior pelvic tilt → Increased lumbar curve → Lower back pain. OR: Tight hips → Limited external rotation → Knee valgus → Meniscus/LCL issues. OR: Tight hips → Reduced abduction → Groin strain.

Three of the most common BJJ injuries. One root cause: tight hips. The 90/90 stretch addresses all of them simultaneously because it works on hip external rotation (front leg) AND internal rotation (back leg) at the same time.

Real talk: I used to think my lower back pain was a back problem. I did every stretch you can imagine for my back. Nothing worked for more than a day. Then I started doing 90/90s daily. After one week, my back pain dropped by 70%. After one month, it was gone. My back wasn't the problem. My hips were.
How to Do the 90/90 Stretch (Proper Form)
Setup

Sit on the floor with your legs in front of you. Bend your right knee to 90 degrees and rotate it outward so your right shin is parallel to the front of your body. Your right knee and ankle should both be on the floor, forming a 90-degree angle. Now place your left leg behind you, also at 90 degrees — your left knee to the side, left shin parallel to the back of your body. Both hip joints should be at 90 degrees.
The Movement
Keep your spine tall — don't collapse forward. Gently lean your torso toward your front shin. Stop when you feel a stretch. Breathe deeply. Hold for 2 minutes. Switch sides.
Common Mistakes

items: Rounding the lower back to reach further — keep the spine long.
Not going deep enough — most grapplers need to get their front shin closer to their body.
Holding your breath — the stretch happens on the exhale.
Bouncing — never bounce. Slow, static holds only.

content.text: The Daily Hip Routine (7 Minutes)
Do this every day. No exceptions. It takes 7 minutes.

items: 90/90 — 2 minutes per side
Pigeon pose — 90 seconds per side (alternative entry to hip external rotation)
Figure 4 stretch (lying down) — 90 seconds per side
Combat base groin stretch — 60 seconds per side

posts.title: 8 Things You Can Do to Prevent 80% of BJJ Injuries
posts.description: Most BJJ injuries are predictable and preventable. After 15 years of training and coaching, I've identified the 8 most effective strategies that keep grapplers on the mats. Do these, and you'll prevent 80% of the injuries that end BJJ careers.
posts.lede: The statistic that keeps me up at night: 96% of people who start BJJ quit. And the #1 reason is injury. Not because they didn't like it. Not because it was too hard. Because their body broke down before their skills caught up. I've been training for 15 years, and I've seen this cycle destroy more potential black belts than anything else. Here's how to be part of the 4% who stay.

content.text: This is the most important article on this site. Read it. Save it. Share it with your training partners. If every grappler followed these 8 rules, the retention rate in BJJ would double.
1. Choose Your Sparring Partner With Care

This is the single biggest factor in BJJ longevity. One bad partner can end your week. A pattern of bad partners can end your career. Learn to say no to rolls. You don't need to be rude — "I'm taking it easy today" is enough. Watch how people roll before you roll with them. The spazzy white belt who goes 100% every round? Let someone else deal with that.
2. Warm Up Your Joints, Not Just Your Muscles

Most BJJ warmups are cardiovascular — jump rope, running, burpees. These get blood flowing but they don't prepare your joints for the specific demands of grappling. A proper BJJ warmup needs joint-specific preparation: neck circles, shoulder CARs (controlled articular rotations), hip CARs, Ankle CARs, spine waves.
3. Tap in Time (Ego Check)

You know the moment. You feel the submission coming. You've got 2 seconds to decide: tap, or try to fight out of it. The right choice is always tap. One extra second of ego can cost you 6 months of recovery. I've tapped to white belts as a black belt. And I've never regretted a single tap.
4. Control Over Speed

The most dangerous grappler on the mats is the one who moves fast without control. Speed generates force. Force without control is a lottery — sometimes you win, sometimes your training partner's knee loses. Train at 60-70% intensity. Reserve the explosive speed for competition preparation.
5. Fight Inflammation With Food
Chronic inflammation is the silent killer of BJJ longevity. Most grapplers don't realize that what they eat directly impacts their recovery. Four foods that fight BJJ inflammation:

items: Turmeric + black pepper — curcumin is one of the most powerful natural anti-inflammatories. Take it daily.
Red cabbage — contains anthocyanins that reduce exercise-induced inflammation.
Parsley — rich in apigenin, a compound that reduces inflammatory markers.
Hibiscus tea — packed with antioxidants, helps muscle recovery after intense training.

content.text: 6. Hydrate Properly

Most grapplers are chronically dehydrated. Dehydrated muscles are more prone to cramping, tearing, and slow recovery. Drink 30ml of water per kg of body weight daily. Add electrolytes before and after training. Avoid alcohol within 24 hours of training — it impairs muscle recovery for 48 hours.
7. Do Proper Recovery After Class
The 30 minutes after BJJ class are the most important 30 minutes of your day. Here's what I do, no exceptions:

items: 10 minutes of light stretching (hip openers, spinal twists, hamstring release).
10 minutes of foam rolling (glutes, quads, lats, thoracic spine).
10 minutes of deep breathing and rehydration.

content.text: 8. 30 Minutes on the Floor Every Day

This is my non-negotiable rule. 30 minutes of mobility work every single day. Not 30 minutes of stretching while watching TV. 30 minutes of focused, intentional movement. The days you feel like skipping are the most important days to do it. Consistency beats intensity.

posts.title: BJJ With Sciatica: 5 Triggers to Avoid and 3 Stretches That Actually Help
posts.description: That sharp, shooting pain down your leg after BJJ isn't a coincidence. Here's exactly what causes sciatica in grapplers, the 5 triggers to eliminate from your game, and the 3 stretches that provide real relief — not temporary distraction.
posts.lede: The first time I felt it, I thought someone had kicked me in the back of the thigh. I looked around — nobody was there. The second time, I was just lying in bed, turning over. The pain shot from my lower back down to my toes like an electric shock. That was my introduction to BJJ sciatica. It took me six months and three different physios to figure out what was actually causing it.

content.text: The BJJ-Specific Cause of Sciatica
Sciatica isn't a condition. It's a symptom — a nerve being compressed or irritated somewhere along its path. In BJJ players, the compression happens in three places:

items: The lumbar spine (disc pressing on the nerve root) — from being stacked, bridging excessively, or years of guard play.
The piriformis muscle (deep in the glute) — from tight hips and constant external rotation demands.
The hamstring origin (sitting on it in closed guard) — from spending hours with your legs wrapped around a partner.

content.text: Most grapplers assume it's the disc. In my experience coaching, it's more often the piriformis or hamstring — which means the treatment is completely different.
5 Training Triggers to Eliminate

items: Getting stacked repeatedly — If someone stacks you, give up the sweep. It's not worth the nerve compression.
Sitting in closed guard for extended rounds — Open your guard frequently. Give your hamstring origins a break.
Inverting — Berimbolos and shoulder rolls compress the lumbar spine. Skip them during flare-ups.
Deep half guard — This position cranks the hip into internal rotation, which can aggravate the piriformis.
Butterfly guard with heavy pressure — The flexion + compression pattern is a sciatica trigger for many grapplers.

content.text: 3 Stretches That Actually Help
1. Piriformis Release (Tennis Ball Technique)

Sit on a tennis ball placed under the belly of your glute (not the bone). Roll slowly until you find the tender spot. Hold for 60 seconds, breathing deeply. This releases the piriformis and takes pressure off the sciatic nerve. Do this after every BJJ session.
2. Nerve Flossing (Slump Test Position)

Sit on the edge of a chair. Slump your spine. Tuck your chin. Extend one leg. Point your toes down. Then slowly point your toes up while looking up. This glides the sciatic nerve through the surrounding tissue and can dramatically reduce symptoms. Repeat 15 times per leg.
3. Supine Figure 4 (Piriformis Stretch)
Lie on your back. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee. Pull the bottom leg toward your chest. Hold 90 seconds per side. This stretches the piriformis without loading the spine.

faq.q: Can I train BJJ with sciatica?
faq.a: Yes, but you need to identify the source first. If it's a disc issue, follow the herniated disc protocol. If it's piriformis or hamstring, the 3 stretches above will help. Stop training if you experience progressive weakness or loss of function.

faq.q: How long does BJJ sciatica last?
faq.a: Acute flare-ups typically last 1-2 weeks with proper management. Chronic cases can persist longer and usually indicate an underlying issue (tight hips, weak core) that needs addressing.

faq.q: Should I see a doctor for BJJ sciatica?
faq.a: Yes, if: the pain is severe, you have numbness or tingling in your foot, you have difficulty walking, or the symptoms last longer than 2 weeks without improvement.

posts.title: Why Am I Not Getting Better at BJJ? The Plateau Isn't a Skill Problem — It's a Body Problem
posts.description: You drill. You roll. You compete. And you're still stuck at the same level. Here's the hard truth: your BJJ plateau is probably not a technique problem. It's a mobility, recovery, and body awareness problem. Here's how to fix it.
posts.lede: You've been training for two years. You know the techniques. You can drill them perfectly. But when you roll, nothing works. Your guard gets passed. You can't retain position. And you have no idea why. I've seen this pattern in hundreds of grapplers. And in almost every case, the problem isn't in your head. It's in your body.

content.text: Why Your Guard Gets Passed
You know the technical adjustment: frame, shrimp, recover guard. But when you try it, your shrimp is two inches too short. Your frame collapses under pressure. Why?

Because the hip mobility you need to shrimp effectively is lacking. Because the thoracic extension you need to frame is restricted. Because your core strength runs out after 30 seconds of fighting for guard retention.

I remember hitting this wall as a purple belt. I couldn't understand why my guard retention was terrible even though I knew all the positions. Then I recorded myself rolling and watched. My shrimp was barely moving me. My hips had maybe 50% of the range they needed. I started doing daily hip mobility work. Two months later, my guard retention had completely transformed. My coach asked what I'd changed. "I stopped trying to learn new techniques and started learning how to move better."
The Mobility-Skill Connection

Here's something most BJJ coaches don't talk about: every technique has a mobility prerequisite. The berimbolo requires hip internal rotation that most adults don't have. The truck roll requires thoracic spine extension. The inverted guard requires at least 90 degrees of hip flexion with a neutral spine.
If you're missing the mobility prerequisite, you can drill the technique a thousand times and it will never work in a live roll. Your body simply can't execute the movement.
The 4 Mobility Tests Every BJJ Player Should Pass

items: The Deep Squat: Can you hold a deep squat with your heels on the ground for 60 seconds? If not, your hip and ankle mobility are limiting your open guard.
The 90/90 Switch: Can you transition from one 90/90 position to the other without using your hands? If not, your hip rotation is insufficient for guard retention.
The Thoracic Extension Test: Lying on your back with a foam roller under your shoulder blades, can you touch your forehead to the floor? If not, your posture is compromising your frames.
The Active Pigeon: In pigeon pose, can you actively bring your front shin closer to your body without rounding your back? If not, your external rotation is limited.

content.text: Your New Training Formula
For the next 12 weeks, shift your focus:

items: 80% of your mat time: drilling and rolling (your Jiu-Jitsu).
15% of your mat time: mobility and body prep (your movement quality).
5% of your mat time: reflection and recording (your awareness).

content.text: Most grapplers spend 0% on the second and third categories. That's why they plateau. When you do the 15%, everything else gets easier.

faq.q: Why do some people improve faster at BJJ?
faq.a: It's rarely about talent. The fast improvers have better body awareness, better mobility, and better recovery habits. These are trainable skills, not genetic gifts.

faq.q: How long does a BJJ plateau last?
faq.a: With traditional training (just drilling and rolling), plateaus can last months or years. With targeted mobility and body awareness work, most grapplers break through in 4-8 weeks.

faq.q: Should I take a break if I'm plateauing?
faq.a: A short break (3-7 days) can help reset your nervous system and allow minor injuries to heal. But the real fix is changing what you do when you train — not training less.
